utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Udo for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour, I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. Delalic is also defended by my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Zeljko Olujic, representing Mr. Mucic today, along with Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, Defence attorney for Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I apologise for being late. I am Cynthia McMurrey and, along with my colleague Nancy Boler, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May I remind the witness, you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath. ILJAS HADZIBEGOVIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Professor, have you had some rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, before we continue today, I am going to just draw your attention to -- please wait for the interpretation of my answer through those earphones and then answer my question, thank you. Yesterday, you testified before this Trial Chamber that the call of Mr. Karadzic in the Bosnian Assembly in October 1991 amounted to a call to arms or an invitation to start a war and you said that you witnessed that and you were a witness to these events. May I now ask the technical booth to play the tape number 2, the excerpt 2. I would like, after that, to ask you a question, professor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Translating videotape). This is what unarmed people are, not armed, the ones over there, this is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you tell us what city this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What location in Sarajevo was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Liberation Square in front of the Bosnian Assembly and this is 6 April 1992, the day when the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed. The citizens of Sarajevo gathered in the square that day, demonstrating for peace. They were asking -- they demanded peace and the shots you heard, these shots were fired by snipers who were placed in surrounding buildings among others on the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, no further details are needed. Is this incident considered the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This event is not the beginning of the war. The war had started earlier, on 6 April in fact the army had already taken positions all around Bosnia, before that time, along with the extremist paramilitary formations from Serbia and, including the Seselj people and the Arkan people. They were already on the ground and they were taking over control of towns. From 27 March until 30 April, a whole string of cities in Posavina, which are the municipalities along the Sava River and the Drina River were taken over and the ethnic cleansing was already under way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, professor. You said this yesterday but I am reminding you of it today. You were a participant of this mass popular demand for peace; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this excerpt, which was used by the witness and which he personally recognised and in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not see its relevance at all. It has nothing to do with the charges for which your client has been charged. It has nothing to do with it. It is background which everybody admits.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are just wasting the time of everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously, you have the right to deny me any single question I ask. My client has been charged as a commander of a Tactical Group and the reason why this Tactical Group was established was Sarajevo. So I would like to request you to listen to me carefully and I am not submitting anything that is not relevant to my client's Defence. I think that, without understanding the situation in Sarajevo at the time, I believe that it would be impossible to understand why Tactical Groups were established, and this is in response to the evidence presented by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it is part of your case, go ahead. I do not see the relevance -- you can prove it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We can take judicial notice of the fact that Sarajevo was under siege -- under Rule 92, we can take judicial notice of the fact that Sarajevo was under siege by the Serb forces, whatever they were. Under Rule 92 we can take judicial notice of that. You do not have to get this tape on the record. In fact, we have seen this tape before also -- I think while you were cross-examining some of the Prosecution witnesses, we saw this portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Whether Sarajevo was under siege is not disputed, is it? The fact that Sarajevo was under siege has never been disputed -- nobody is arguing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had tried to offer this into evidence through a Defence witness, and then I was told that I was to do this through the Prosecution witness and I was told to do it during my own case, so I am trying to speed up these proceedings as much as I can, but, hangar 6, for instance, is very important for this case, but it is not that important for my client in the sense that he was never there. We must discuss matters that my client was involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not opposing it if you think it is part of your case, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I indicate something -- the fact that there was an armed conflict is not disputed -- it has never been disputed. This is only evidence of that. I should say that I do not know what is going to happen with these tapes but one of them goes for two hours. Are we going to sit and watch it for two hours?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is why I am showing two minutes so that we would not be looking at two hours, so I would like only to introduce this excerpt and maybe another two more. This is all that I am trying to do, but I am going to tender the entire tape in the same manner that Dr. Calic's tapes were produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The facts are not in dispute -- it is unnecessary to bring it into issue. Nobody is arguing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There are at least two Resolutions of the Security Council talking about the siege of Sarajevo, one of 15 May and the other of 30 May. We can take judicial notice of the fact that Sarajevo was under siege and efforts were being made to lift that siege. We do not need an expert witness to tell us that. These facts are well known. The Resolution of the Security Council is something of which we can take judicial notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I feel very awkward to start discussing this with you, but, in the Tadic case, the Trial Chamber watched six or seven hours of the BBC programmes on Yugoslavia. Maybe it was not as necessary for Omarska, but I am just trying to do the relevant things for my client. I cannot repeat whether he was responsible for Jablanica, Prozor or Igman. This is what we have to demonstrate through our evidence, whether he was involved and what he was doing. We are trying to show why he was part of this Tactical Group -- because of what was going on in Sarajevo. I only need five minutes of videotape rather than two hours like my colleague is saying, so I am trying to present it as rationally as possible, and not make it just a part of general information on what was going on in Bosnia. So, I do apologise for this discussion with you, but I would urge you to allow me to present it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object if the tape -- the whole tape is sought to be tendered on the basis of a four-minute excerpt being played, because the whole of the tape -- if Madam Residovic is trying to get in a whole tape just on the basis of a two-minute excerpt, I object to that. I also wish to indicate that I sat through the Tadic case and at no stage do I remember six hours of videotape being played by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was trying to tender this particular excerpt into evidence rather than a two-hour tape. I am only going to introduce three excerpts from this tape into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Frankly, any portion about the siege of Sarajevo does not prejudice your case. These are accepted facts and undisputed. I do not see why you make so much fuss about it. Nobody is arguing that Sarajevo was under siege. Nobody is arguing that there was an effort to lift the siege. Why do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is opposing views that there were no Tactical Groups, so this is just by way of introducing our defence of where our client was and what he was doing. This is what the Prosecution had started with, the context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The videotape will not demonstrate whether or not there was a Tactical Group. It cannot show that. It will not be evidence of that. That is a different situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: By alleging that Mr. Delalic was commander of the Tactical Group, the Prosecution concedes there were Tactical Groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If all you are interested in is to give a story -- perhaps this is what you are trying to do here, you are trying to tell a story -- the story is interesting if it is relevant to what you are saying and if it is disputed. There is no dispute here. I have avoided this argument not to waste time -- if you want to get it in, that is okay, but it is not relevant at all -- it has nothing to do with the issue. It is only disputed issues that ought to be proven. If they are not disputed, they have been accepted, so what is the point?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, allow me to say just one thing. I would like you to respect our right to defend provided in Article 21 of the Statute. You have admitted a number of tapes that are not relevant for this issue, and which have nothing to do with the Tactical Groups or their existence. You said that you will evaluate its probative value, but if the Prosecution tendered it, you have at least accepted to rule on it. I also would like you to apply the same criteria to what we are trying to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not like the imputation that one is favouring one party to the other. There is no such thing. If you really understand the case you are building, you would have understood what I have said. I have said this is not disputed, and there is no point telling the story. But, if you still think that your story is palatable to your own case, yes, go ahead, but I do not see the basis for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I ask you whether the excerpt that we just played is being admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: As giving the story of certain people making protests in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the reason why the military authorities adopted the decision to change, that is, as part of an attempt to come to a solution of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Go ahead. Carry on with your case. Go ahead with your case, present it as best you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell me the number of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D142/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your report and the documents attached, you mentioned the concept of "ethnic cleansing". What did that actually mean in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Ethnic cleansing" entered a political programme during the Second World War; that is, the expression itself. In that programme, it implied cleansing of territories, which were considered to be of Serb interest, of all non-Serb inhabitants. The same term appeared in this war, except that it is an euphemism for killing and brutal expulsions of non-Serb populations from certain territories.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask the technicians to show the map H1/10, for me to be able to put the next question to the witness. Can we see the map, please -- H1/10? Professor, could you explain this map for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina drawn by a professor at the faculty of law in Sarajevo -- a prestigious expert on the basis of his analysis of two documents of the Serbian and Croatian extremist leadership, that is of the SDS and the HDZ. You saw the map that I showed yesterday about the ethnic composition of Bosnia. It was coloured in different colours. On this map you see the red and white areas with no other colours. Then you see the blue colour, which indicates territories captured by Herceg-Bosna -- the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The red and white ones -- areas were captured by Serbs and Serb autonomous regions were formed, whereas the yellow colour indicates areas where the interests of both political groupings overlap, whereas the white enclaves are still territories shared by everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we compare these two maps, we see that, in order to obtain one colour, other colours had to be deleted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did that really mean in those wartime days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It meant the creation of ethnically pure territories.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after this question, I have only two clips to show from the videotape which I have offered, but, before that, let me put a question to the professor. At the beginning of May, was Sarajevo completely cut off from the rest of the world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask the technical booth to show us clips 5, 6 and 7, and you will see from the questions that they are directly related to the defence of my client. May I ask the technical booth to show clips 5, 6 and 7, please? Can we see the video clips, please? Before they start, will you please tell me whether the central and main post office in Sarajevo was destroyed at a certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 2 May, the main post office was set on fire and about 50 to 60 telephone lines were cut.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did this result in the city of Sarajevo being totally cut off from the other parts of the republic and the world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were other important cultural establishments, archives, et cetera, also destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a little later, in August, the National and University Library was set on fire; then the Oriental Institute was burned down, with its archives of original 250,000 documents and its library as well as other institutions, especially the Presidency was exposed to shelling, the 20-storey building of the Government, the university departments, hospitals -- all these institutions were exposed to heavy shelling from the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after those events, how could a message be sent -- a message or an order -- from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the help of a few radio amateurs that existed, all of our citizens who had our children elsewhere sent messages through radio amateurs, if we were lucky to find them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now be shown these video clips 5, 6 and 7, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the main post office in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the most beautiful buildings in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you recognise this building, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the National and University Library in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hundreds of thousands of books went up in flames. It is a building constructed at the end of the 19th century, in pseudo-Moorish style.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, we do not need those details, professor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to tender these three clips into evidence -- that is all that we ask from this videotape and the grounds are the position of my client regarding the receipt of certain orders and this videotape is indicative of the conditions that existed in respect of communications between Sarajevo and other parts of the republic. So, may I please tender these three clips into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object on the grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They are not really relevant, but, if you want to tender them, let us admit them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please tell me the numbers of the exhibits that have been tendered into evidence just now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They will be part of Exhibit D142/1 and will be specifically marked as segments 2, 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let us now go on to another subject. Can you tell me, from the beginning of the war until the end of 1992, what was the policy of the Croatian Democratic Unity, that is, one of the winning Parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian Democratic Alliance in Bosnia-Herzegovina cooperated with the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, and they entered the war together. At a referendum, they voted together and their interests coincided, because, had the referendum failed, Bosnia-Herzegovina would have been within the frameworks of a Greater Serbia and this did not suit either of them. So, they had common interests at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you tell me how this overall situation, bearing in mind the history we referred to since 1980, affect relations and events in Konjic? But, first, I should like you to tell us something briefly about the geopolitical position of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Konjic is one of the oldest towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, in fact, in the whole of the former Yugoslavia. It is situated in the area of upper Herzegovina, that is, northern Herzegovina, on both banks of a river linking Bosnia with the Adriatic, or, rather, linking the Danube basin, the centre of the Balkans, with the Mediterranean. Konjic, due to its great significance in terms of communications, strategy and trade, became very important in the political plans of both Croatia and the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what are the ethnic characteristics of Konjic municipality? To illustrate this, I should like to ask the technicians to show us map H1/11?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an ethnic map of the municipality of Konjic, using the same procedure as the other ethnic map that you saw yesterday, and it uses the same colours, reflecting the multi-ethnic composition of Konjic municipality. According to the 1991 census, the municipality of Konjic had a population of 43,878 inhabitants, out of which about 48 per cent -- sorry, 54 per cent were Bosniaks, 26 per cent were Croats, and 15 per cent were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the majority of settlements within the Konjic municipality with a mixed population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is typical of Konjic. It is a municipality which is hilly -- it has 148 settlements, but most in 1879 and 1910, according to the censuses of those days, most of the settlements were ethnically mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you show us map H1/12 to explain what you are just telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is also a map of Konjic municipality showing the communes that were ethnically pure -- the communes or settlements that were ethnically pure. The blue indicates the Bosniaks; the red or brown -- I do not know what it looks like as you see it -- are Croats; and the yellow are Serbs and the pale blue colour indicates mixed populations in the territory of this municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you tell us whether you know what the results of the assembly elections for the municipal assembly of Konjic were in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They roughly corresponded to the victory of the nationalist parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The same occurred in Konjic. The SDA won 28 out of the 60 seats, SDA -- I am sorry, SDS in 9 -- in percentages the SDA had 35.-something, the Croats had 17.-something and the Serbs 15 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, I think I have the percentages wrong. The percentages are not so important. They can be found in the evidence already admitted. In order to put my next question, could the professor be given this binder, so that we could comment on the organisation of authority in the municipality? (Handed) Will you please, professor, look at your annex D7? We have the table that you made, so could you please place it under the ELMO, or, since we all have a copy, we can look at it together. It is D7 -- have you found it, professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This annex that is being shown is marked D136/1 and, within the binder, it is D7. Could you please explain what this chart depicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This chart depicts the pre-war organisation of Government in the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that organisation different from the same institutions in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was more or less the same as in other municipalities. There are some minor differences -- not in Konjic but in some other municipalities, which were smaller and they had fewer bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, which were the executive bodies and which were the regulatory or legislative bodies in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the constitutional legal reforms, which lasted and which were carried out from 1980 until 1991, there was tripartite authority introduced in Bosnia-Herzegovina, legislative executive and judiciary. On this chart we see the municipal assembly, which had the function of a regulatory institution, that is, one that passes regulations. Then the executive powers were held in the executive board, which had its own administrative bodies, or the municipal administration. Then we have several vertical lines here (indicates). First, the public security service or the police, which was directly subordinate to the centre of security services, and the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is not subordinate to the municipal assembly, but only cooperates with it. The second vertical line shows the defence department. It, too, was subordinate directly to the Defence Ministry of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this dotted line going towards the municipal assembly indicates the cooperation between the municipal assembly and this department. The third vertical line is the basic court -- it is the municipal court which was completely separate from the municipal assembly and it was subordinate to the higher court and the supreme court, or, rather, the Ministry of Justice. All these institutions that were subordinate to the ministries were financed out of the republic's budget and did not depend on the municipality. The judges were appointed by the Ministry of Justice in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, we see that there was also a rather special court, and that is the Magistrates Court, which is an administrative court, which tried minor offences and misdemeanours and its jurisdiction was to sentence someone to 60 days in prison and fines, for traffic offences and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that is the organisation of authority before the war broke out. Tell us, since you told us that the SDS was also one of the victorious parties in the Konjic municipality, did the SDS of Konjic implement the policies of the SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina that you spoke about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it implemented the policies of the SDS and it was also incorporated into the legal organs of authority. If I may, it was incorporated until the last session, the 9th session of the municipal assembly, after which, two days after that, they walked out of the municipal assembly bodies -- all the bodies, except the public security service, which they abandoned later on and formed their own service.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, professor, whether your research has shown that, in their illegal or semi-legal activities the SDS passed decisions proclaiming parts of the municipality Serb territories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 22 March the so-called assembly of the Serbian municipality formed the territory of the Serbian municipality. It did so on the basis of two principles. It took the settlements with a Serb majority -- that was that Serbs accounted for more than 50 per cent of the population -- that was one principle -- and the other principle was property ownership. Wherever there was any property owned by Serb households, these were proclaimed Serb territories, and these villages were registered as being in the Serbs' interests and such villages and settlements in the municipality of Konjic were a total of 40, taking both principles as a basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you have made a chart of these decisions of the Serbian municipality, so could we please see that map, too, H1/13?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have that map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Has the technical department shown us this map -- H1/13? That is the new map -- do you have this map now on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this reflect their decision to divide the municipality and to take control of areas as you have just told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Could you tell me whether your research has shown that the legal authorities in Konjic municipality, after the decision of the Presidency of the republic to proclaim an immediate threat of war -- did they undertake certain defensive measures? What do you know about those measures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The constitution envisaged that, when an immediate threat of war is proclaimed, or a state of war, the conditions were in place for a different organisation of authority. After the proclamation of an immediate threat of war, changes were introduced in the organisation of authority, and a war presidency was formed. Prior to this, a crisis staff existed for a short while, but the war presidency was introduced later, and this was provided for in the constitution, so this was automatic, and this war presidency was a substitute for the municipal assembly, because it had regulatory powers -- what the municipal assembly had before that -- but the war presidency, or the presidency of the municipal assembly -- it was referred to as the war presidency -- it held its meetings and passed regulations with the effect of law for as long as the conditions were such that the assembly could not meet. If conditions were normal, then the assembly had to confirm those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, after the beginning of the war on 6 April, was a meeting of the assembly held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 9th session was the last to be held with all the elected deputies taking part -- not all of them, but at least all the parties that won seats participated and this meeting was held on 17 April and that session had a large agenda, but most important among the items were two. One regarding the abolition of the former Territorial Defence leadership and the formation of a new one, and the appointment of a new head of the Territorial Defence staff, whose appointment needed to be confirmed by the republic. The Serb deputies also participated -- out of 9 elected members, six participated. They voted against the formation of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell me whether, after the new Territorial Defence was formed, which you have just spoken about, the changes of the organisation of local government also took place and since you drafted another chart, could you please show us what changes took place, looking at that chart which is D9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here is the chart of the organisation of Government in the municipality during the war and during the immediate threat of war. So, the municipal assembly has now been replaced by the war presidency and, as you can see, these full and broken lines remained where they were before, which means that the key change was really the substitution of the municipal assembly, which was unable to meet. So, only a smaller number of people could meet and this war presidency takes over the powers which had the municipal assembly. The other bodies, as far as their subordination and their co-operation, pretty much remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in this chart I see an additional body, which earlier was not separate, and I guess it was because it was peace time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the Territorial Defence and the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the assembly reorganised the power and created this new body and its commander. Could you tell me what this line then signifies there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This perpendicular line shows that the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence and Territorial Defence units are not subordinated to the presidency, but, rather, to the district staff of the Territorial Defence and the main staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us, in 1992 in Konjic, was the district headquarters staff in Mostar in existence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To whom then was this staff subordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was subordinated directly to the republican staff or the main staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. This map, there is one line missing, the one you said that was directly responsible to the TO -- not the district staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, there is a line here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is one missing in the chart supplied to me. This line is missing here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible -- your Honours, do you have the line that is being shown on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No, I do not have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the TO units. My apologies. Can we substitute it with another copy? My apologies, this would just be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Show it to Madam Residovic. He will show you the line which is missing to which you are referring -- subordination to the district staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the usher can show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I raise a matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My understanding is that this material which is now being shown to the professor was admitted on the basis that it represented what he relied upon in order to prepare his report. By showing it to him now and going into the detail in which they are going, it is certainly going beyond that basis of admissibility and going into the area of the document being admitted for the truth of its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is a document prepared him just to show what the organisation was in Konjic, and he has prepared it himself. That is why she is introducing it into evidence -- something he studied and the chart which he prepared himself, just like we admitted certain charts made by Dr. Calic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand that, but the position is that, somehow or other, the basis of admissibility seems to have changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not sure. We admitted Dr. Calic's charts, which she prepared herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not talking about Dr. Calic. What happens with another witness, depending on the position taken by the Defence and the ruling of your Honours, cannot automatically just apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not automatically, no. This is material provided for us and to you to support the basis on which he prepared his report so you can cross-examine him with reference to that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In my submission, it is going beyond that now, by this witness speaking to it in the way that he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You will notice that was missing from the chart which I got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness has not said anything about the document he relied upon -- he said nothing about it, if that is what he relied upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he said this line here represents the fact that the public security station is subordinate to the Minister of the Interior and drawing attention to those lines there, that goes beyond saying, "This is a document which I relied on in order to express my opinion." He is asserting by that that this document is admitted for the truth of its contents, namely, that the Ministry of the Interior is superior to the public security station. It takes it into a different category of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not if he is the author of this particular document itself. He is presenting what he has done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was under the misapprehension that all of this material, which was admitted in bulk, was admitted on the basis that it merely went to show the basis upon which he relied upon it. I am not so concerned about this chart, but I notice the way it is being handled suggests that it is being admitted for the truth, so there has been an automatic jump to that point without any basis being presented by the Defence as to why it should be. There has not been one word said, as far as I can recall, about the fact that he himself prepared it, other than it is written on the document. I do not recall him saying that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Take it as a whole, made by --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I could have done that. That would not have made it so -- I could have typed it on myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The reliability of this document depends on the reliability of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is so, but there are numerous documents in here which we challenge. I am just wishing to make the point that, when it comes to those documents, I wish to raise my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you are perfectly right. When a document is represented for a particular purpose, we have to know the authority under which it is being represented. So if he is the author of that document, then he could say so, and then we treat it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As far as I know, he has not said so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my apologies to you, because obviously one of the lines was obviously omitted on one of the copies of the charts, and as I pointed out, the professor did consult all the relevant documents when preparing these charts. I have still not tendered these documents -- I have just had them marked for identification. Right now we are going through them and the witness is explaining how he arrived at certain charts. Now that we have, I believe, resolved the technical problem relating to the chart -- do you have the good copy of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I have it now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I would like now to take you to the material which you used to prepare your report and which relates to the war presidency and the activities in Konjic in early 1992. Can you tell us whether, during your research, you found documents relating to the war presidency activity -- decisions of that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the supporting materials, I have provided a document which is very characteristic of their work and it is dated 3 June 1992. From these minutes of the meeting of the presidency, you can glean the range and the scope of questions that the war presidency handled at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please quote some of the issues that were handled by the war presidency in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It handled various issues relating to the daily life of the local population. This was a session held after the events in Bradina and Donje Selo -- the presidency, the presidency orders that these areas be repaired, that the medical care be provided -- and examination be provided to the prisoners there, that blankets be provided for them, and this is in Celebici and then, as far as the town itself is concerned, various economic issues -- the provision of food. Since there is no money, the food stamps are introduced, so the presidency tackles a whole range of issues and I have provided a document -- the document which states what decisions were taken at that time and who was to implement them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The minutes of that session, which you have just mentioned, are enclosed in the supporting materials -- there are 22 decision that were taken there. Were any decisions taken then which relate to the commanding of the units of the Territorial Defence there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not find any such decisions. These were only decisions that related to the accommodation, provision of food, acquiring of uniforms -- so, these are the types of decisions. There is no decision on control and command. It would be something that the civilian government would do in a situation like that, as set out by law. There is not a single decision that relates to the control or command of the military units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, during the research that you conducted in preparation of this report, did your research provide you with an answer to the question as to whether the war presidency was a civilian or a military structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From these minutes, it is clear that the municipal assembly is a civilian body and the war presidency is also by extension a civilian body and so it only handles the issues that the municipal assembly handled in peace time. Obviously the conditions have changed now -- they were wartime conditions -- but the essence did not change; they only adopted the decisions that belonged to the civilian government.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, by researching different documents from archives in Konjic, could you determine whether the war presidency in this period was highly involved in these civilian-type matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was very involved in such matters, because, in Konjic -- Konjic was a cross-roads. The refugees were coming through from both eastern Bosnia and eastern Herzegovina, which additionally burdened the already stretched resources for both accommodation and food and also, in this period, this town was heavily shelled and it was considered one of the four or five worst affected towns in Bosnia that way. There was a large number of refugees. This included people who had been ethnically cleansed and who found refuge in and around the town, so there was an unbearable pressure being exercised and there were these large numbers of people from eastern Bosnia, who did not know where to go and what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, among the documents that you have submitted, there are also some documents which were provided to you by the Defence, including a document of 18 May as to the appointment of Zejnil Delalic as a co-ordinator of the Territorial Defence and war presidency. My question to you is does this position of co-ordinator imply a position of superior authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the material that I have discovered, I have not found -- I could not find anything that would show me that, within the structure of any kind of power, there is provision of co-ordination, so the position of co-ordinator that Mr. Delalic was appointed to is something that was created out of a desperate situation that the town found itself in. So, you have major problems of feeding the population, a huge number of refugees, and also the war presidency had a major task of organising the defence. You had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. The witness is a professor of history. How did he know who was a co-ordinator?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am satisfied with his answer that he could not find a document which would define the position of "co-ordinator" and I believe that it is not necessary to go further into it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have consulted the documents. There are no provisions for a co-ordinator, but there is nothing that prevents it. It was something that was usual, to co-ordinate in conditions when the regular institutions have broken down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just answered my next questions. I was going to ask you whether, in this report or in this research of yours, you found whether this was provided by law and then, given the conditions, were some new bodies created which assisted the war presidency and which involved these co-ordinators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were other bodies as well, like the civilian protection -- there were other bodies which had the right and task to assist. But I am afraid I may not have fully understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, professor, you created these charts. You were looking at the very recent history relating to the activities of the war presidency and, in this capacity, could you tell me whether this civilian body which appointed Zejnil Delalic could appoint him to any military position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it could not have done so, because the military authorities would make such appointments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The next question could be answered by just about anyone, so I am not going to ask you whether a body can appoint someone who would be its superior. However, let us move on. In your research, have you found information that, in 1992, a certain group of people was detained in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the Institute for Research of War Crimes, I was able to see a document relating to the list of people who were questioned in Celebici, because this was actually a significant part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Had you heard of Celebici before this research?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had not heard of Celebici as a prison before I undertook this research.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, during the war, had some prisons -- are you aware of any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of it, because I had one right across the street -- it was the military prison and military court in Sarajevo, which was in the barracks, and it was also the Military Geographic Institute, so I am away of the fact that there was a military court and a military prison in Sarajevo during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in researching the conditions in the country at the beginning of the war and as a historian, were you able to find any documents which would show that the legal authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- had introduced any type of camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with what the Bassiouni Commission found. I think it was a very fair report, where it says that all three sides in the conflict, that is, it states that the Serbian forces, through the systematic violations, it was part of their plan to conduct ethnic cleansing; that also the Croatian side led by the extremists also engaged in this. Of course, Bassiouni's Commission also contains a view that the legal forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Bosniak forces, which are the Defence forces of the legal authorities, that they, too, were engaged in serious violations, but that it was not out of a plan -- it was not a plan of their waging the war, that is, the violation of international law, to engage in ethnic cleansing, to commit crimes against innocent populations and such. So, my conclusion is that these were exercises rather than a plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question was a bit different. As a historian, you have the right to rely on any source in submitting your views, and so you mentioned the Bassiouni Commission report, but did you find any document which would speak to the fact that the legal authorities in Konjic had created a camp -- did you find any such document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not find any such document, nor do I believe -- no, I did not find any such document which would speak of camps. In Konjic it was a problem of space. Konjic did not have a prison; they had to accommodate a large number of people somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, professor, did you find any decision on the establishment of a prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you consulted with the institute for the investigation of war crimes. Can you say, based on the documents you saw, how many people were detained in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that I wanted to establish this fact, I was not able to do so. According to what I saw, and it is possible that I did not find all the existing materials -- it could be that certain documents were either destroyed or lost relating to certain prisoners, but, based on what I saw, there could have been about 200 to 250 prisoners there -- up to 300 at the most. Obviously, the number varies. The number was largest after the events in Bradina and Donje Selo and later it diminishes, so it could have been up to 300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we can break now and come back at 12 noon. -- recesses taken at 11.30 a.m. -- on resuming at 12.04 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still under the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I remind you, Sir, that you still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you said that reviewing the documents of the institute for investigating crimes in Sarajevo, you found a quantity of data on persons detained in Celebici. Please, can you tell me, by reviewing those documents, were you able to reach a conclusion as to who those persons were, about whom those documents were that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were citizens and inhabitants of the municipality of Konjic, mostly from the village of Bradina, Donje Selo and Podunavlje - mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Among those documents, did you find data as to whether any criminal proceedings were being conducted against those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There are quite a number of reports on investigations and then, later on, there are 105 criminal charges against persons for criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Attached to your report are a number of court rulings on the discontinuation of those proceedings. Can you tell us what they are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was an amnesty proclaimed by the legal authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- not because those people were not guilty, but because they did so out of mercy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, will you please tell me, on the basis of your research and study of the material at your disposal, could you see whether those people were members of the Yugoslavia People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were they in uniform -- are there data about such things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them had uniforms, but they did not have any insignia. It is not recorded anywhere that anybody had any rank or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you see among those documents whether they were armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were brought there on charges that they had been armed, and it was recorded that most of them had military weapons and that they were putting armed resistance against the legal army, that is the Territorial Defence, the HVO and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your research, professor, lead you to make any conclusions whether those persons were citizens of Konjic or did they come from other towns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were mostly local people -- villagers and some people from town. There were parts of the town where they lived -- they were people whose families had lived there for 100 years, some of them even longer, so there is no doubt as to that. They were local inhabitants of the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your research answer the question whether those people were citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not an expert for citizenship issues. As far as I am concerned, I was a national of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a national of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and, according to the 1974 Bosnia-Herzegovina constitution, the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina are citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object to that. The witness has said that he is not an expert then proceeds to give an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is talking about himself now. He said so far as he is concerned he is a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also under the 1974 constitution, he was a citizen of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not want to pursue it. He was called as an expert witness. Then he says he is not an expert and then proceeds to give an opinion on something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As to himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So long as it is limited to that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The professor has explained his position by referring to a certain document and he is able to say that as a scholar. He said that the 1974 constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- could you repeat what that constitution says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The constitution stipulates that the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina are citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also citizens of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. From the Defence department, I received certain certificates on the citizenship of individual detainees, and I checked them in the Konjic municipality, where they are registered as citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this can be checked -- there is no problem there. According to the Dayton treaty, there is this nationality of Bosnia-Herzegovina which has continuity -- whose continuity has been recognised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, did your research lead you to conclude anything about the kind of prison Celebici was? Was it a civilian or a military prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I am not an expert on prisons, but I was not able to establish it -- I think there were several agencies that had competence over that prison, so it is very difficult to establish. For a time it was a civilian prison, then a military one, then, later, it became a prison over which the police and the army had control, then the higher court, which grants amnesty and so on, so it is really very difficult to be very specific about that and I do not feel competent to go into any further details regarding that, or to make any far-reaching conclusions. If I may, if you wish --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you said that you were not competent on this area. I cannot expect an expert to voice an opinion about things he is not competent for. You have told us what your conclusions were on the basis of your research and I thank you for it. As you said earlier on, you went to the Konjic municipality to do your research in various institutions. Professor, can you please tell us whether you learned what the general situation was in the recent history, that is, during the six months while the prison existed, what was the situation like in Konjic and what were the conditions under which the inhabitants of Konjic lived?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think he answered this question yesterday. He said there were food shortages and there were refugees coming in and there were shortages of everything. I think he said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. I will now ask a more specific question, which was not answered yesterday. There was yesterday mention of food and today of refugees but now I should like to ask you whether, in that period of time, there was a certain number of civilians exposed to injuries, wounding, killings -- did you discover any facts along those lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hospital in Konjic provided data on the persons who were wounded and killed. They gave data on civilian and military casualties. These data are incomplete, because there were several hundred in the group of soldiers -- I cannot recall exactly the numbers -- they can be found in my report. I think about 400 or 450 civilians and about 1,200 wounded or killed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, we have seen the videos and we also have discussed Sarajevo under siege. Could you tell us, on the basis of your overall research, including what you did in preparation of this report, why was the lifting of the siege of Sarajevo so important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sarajevo is, above all, the centre and the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is where the central State institutions are situated, and the question of Sarajevo was really the question of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many people were living in Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 300,000 in a cauldron surrounded by hills and from it was impossible to leave -- the only way out was across the runway controlled by the UNPROFOR. At the same time this is an open space exposed to Serb snipers who were killing people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So your final conclusion, please, linked to this fact of the surrounded Sarajevo, tell me, do you, as a scholar, consider that all the human, military and other reasons existed for each individual and State body to try and lift the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those of us who were in enclosed Sarajevo felt that most acutely. I think this is something that is self-evident. Both people inside and outside wanted and kept trying to lift the siege, but the system was so firm that it was simply impossible to make a breakthrough without international aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we will now move on to the last group of questions that I intended to put to you. As we go through your report and the supporting material that you relied on in preparing that report and your testimony, tell me, professor, before this engagement, did you know any of the persons who are accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know any one of the accused and I saw them for the first time here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the war, or before the war, had you ever heard of Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had not heard of Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In preparing your expert report and leafing through the documents that you found on the ground, did you come across any data about Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Actually, I am asking whether you checked in any way the fact whether Zejnil Delalic was a member of any body in the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the information I received in Konjic, he was not officially a member of any organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn whether he was a member of any political organisation in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I am talking about -- he was not a member of any political organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you have attached the Statute of the war presidency, some of its conclusions and decisions, did you come across any information that would indicate that Zejnil Delalic was a member of the war presidency of the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could not have been a member of the war presidency, because that was prescribed by law. He could only have been invited to attend a meeting of the presidency, but he certainly was not a member of that presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Reviewing the documents in the possession of the Defence, you probably learned some other facts. Did you at all go into the question of Zejnil Delalic's appointment to any military function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I saw the order appointing him commander of Tactical Group 1, and his subsequent appointment to another post, I saw that order, too -- as deputy commander for logistics in Group South. That is all that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you come across any data that would lead you to believe with certainty when Zejnil Delalic left Konjic and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go into that issue. He simply disappeared from Konjic and I was not able to follow that from the materials I examined -- perhaps a military expert could do that better than I.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the documents at your disposal refer to subsequent activities of Zejnil Delalic after he left Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my expert report, I did not take that into consideration, because I did not have the relevant data for that. That would have to be investigated where Mr. Delalic was, and I did not go into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you please tell me whether you know that, in Austria, there is an association of Bosnians of the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there is a club -- I even visited it once in Vienna -- we called it the Bosnian club. That is what people told me -- it is a Bosnian club. I did not even know what its exact name was. We just went to see the place where Bosnians gathered. But I did not know it was a club of Democratic Action. It was a club that Bosnians frequented .

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as you had personal experience, did you, on that occasion, or later, in preparation of this report, know that that club was a political Party of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there is no SDA in Austria, because there cannot be a foreign political Party working legally in another State. Therefore, the Democratic Action Party could not, either, and I read that Alija Izetbegovic, that there are no parties but there are other forms of activity, cultural associations and so on, but no political activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, professor. Your Honours, I have completed my examination of this witness. I should now like to, in line with the procedure applied by this Trial Chamber when adopting the report and documents of witness Dr. Calic, I would now tender into evidence the report, the expert report of professor Dr. Hadzibegovic, that we take judicial notice of the list of documents as already admitted evidence from the report of Dr. Calic, which this expert has referred to, because attached to his expert report, there is a review of the documents that he used and included in his own documents as the basis for his own expert opinion. Third, that we admit into evidence the maps and all the charts, which have been clarified by the witness in this courtroom and, finally, that we admit into evidence the other documents contained in the folder as documents on the basis of which this expert has compiled his expert report and opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object, your Honours. I object. At least some of the documents have been shown to the professor and, insofar as they are concerned, we now have some understanding perhaps of the source of some of them. The vast bulk of the documents, we do not anything about the source of them; we know nothing about the truth of their contents. All we know is that they are material which the professor says apparently he has relied upon for the purposes of his opinion. Again, at this stage, we have said that our objection is not directed to that basis of admissibility. Our objection is directed to them being admitted and, in particular, with respect to specific documents, to them being admitted for the truth of their contents. Your Honours, if we are to comply with what happened in relation to Dr. Calic -- as I understand it, I was not here at the time -- but as I understand it the documents were not admitted until after cross-examination, so it is not in accordance with what happened there, and it is simply not appropriate to say, "Well, there was no objection in relation to Dr. Calic, therefore we rely on that practice and they automatically become admissible." That is not the appropriate basis. If an objection is raised, as your Honours know, the Defence must deal with the objection, and, your Honours, our position has been, right from the outset, that it is because we were confronted with all this material that we have not had, and still have not had the opportunity to finally determine which ones we are prepared to simply say, "We have no objection to them going into evidence." Indeed, in relation to a number of them, we would not have any objection -- in some cases we fail to see the relevance of them, but, if the Defence feel that they somehow or other are central to their case and want to argue that, that is a matter for them. It increases the burden of work for your Honours, but we will not raise serious objection to it. There is a category of these documents which are nothing more than Madam Residovic writing to some institution, whether it be in Konjic or somewhere else, asking for information and getting a letter in reply from them saying, "Zejnil Delalic is not a member of the SDA" or some similar such thing, and she is trying to seek to tender it in this way. We object to that, and we object to it because if they want to establish that, and it is important for them to establish that, then they should call the person from that particular institution who can come along and tell us that. We are then given the opportunity to cross-examine on it. So, your Honours, my suggestion at this stage is that at least the admissibility issue be determined after cross-examination is completed and, hopefully, we can be slightly more helpful in terms of being able to say to you, "Well, in relation to all of these documents, we have no objection, and we just ground our objection in relation to the following ones." That is our submission, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you recall, there were many objections regarding the evidence of Dr. Calic. I remember I objected to all the charts of Dr. Calic regarding the position and mutual relationships of bodies and the question of a co-ordinator. You admitted those documents, but you said that we could establish those facts in our case and each time you admitted evidence, you reminded us of the Rules of this Tribunal, according to which, if a party is able to contest the document, that it can always do so by referring to Rule 89 and 92 subsequently. I have again studied very closely the procedure we went through at the time, and I think, by tendering the evidence in this way, I am fully respectful of your rulings in that case. There is no difference here with respect to the previous expert. The only difference is that this expert has been called by the Defence and the last time it was the Prosecution who called the witness. But I think from the standpoint of the Trial Chamber, this is identical and, as you have said many times, we are absolutely equal before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that your answer to the criticisms? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There are still so many open-ended things. There is the expert report, which the expert himself has produced. In addition to that, there are the annexes to that report. If you look at the annexes, there are so many areas you might have mentioned in your examination-in-chief which you might have relied upon, and there are other areas which have not been touched and there are also areas where they have been in a different language, which do not appear to have been translated, or, if translated, there is nothing to show that they have been. The difficulty is how you relate this to the report and, for the purposes of admissibility, whether you can rely on this -- not only by the expert himself but also by each of those who want to rely on these annexes for the purposes of his report. I do not think the question of his report would be very seriously challenged, because he is here himself to authenticate it and admit that he is the author of the report. When it comes to the annexes and maps -- some produced by him, others perhaps not by him -- they also have their own difficulties. I am not prepared to go into what you said about Dr. Calic and the like, because my recollection of Dr. Calic is that the chart was produced by the expert herself. I do not see you can argue with somebody who said, "I produce this chart and I rely on it for the purposes of my report." They are quite different things. Here, there are annexes which perhaps might require explanation. It is not the same thing. You might be able to distinguish the expert report itself from the documents which you now rely upon for the purposes of the reports and those documents which you have not even referred to at all. You referred to some of them and, as the Prosecutor has pointed out, some of the reports might have been letters in reply to your own queries and written by somebody who is not here to say whether he wrote them or not. There is quite a lot of explanation to make in respect of it. To take a document like this (indicating) and admit it without knowing exactly what it is, that is a fairly difficult thing to do. As I said, it is a different thing with the expert reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you have asked me whether that was my complete answer before your comments, I thought that I had answered, but now I understand you better. I am tendering the report as evidence straight away, because the witness has covered the whole report through my questions. Secondly, I really have to refer again to the previous procedure, and I immediately propose that although this witness has confirmed that he has checked each of my letters in the municipality, I propose that those documents should not be admitted at all -- there are four or five of them. Thirdly, in Dr. Calic's binder, there are documents which I personally gave to the Prosecution and which the Prosecution gave to Dr. Calic, and no-one at that stage checked how come Dr. Calic had a document which I had given the Prosecution. So, that was the attitude towards the relevancy of documents which she used to base her opinion on. Briefly, in annex 1, which has been submitted to you, it contains literature, laws and all the things that Professor Hadzibegovic has told us about. It is the historical materials he has been working with for years, and which he used to make an assessment of the present period. Therefore, annex 1 only, under item 11, has a table, which, as can be seen from that table or chart, is one that the professor himself made on the basis of his own research. Therefore, that annex, in its entirety, can be admitted already today. As for annex B, in this annex, taking into account the explanation he gave, the professor said that he used the specific documents used by Dr. Calic, and he incorporated them in his expert report and those are official gazettes and the material of the Institute for the Study of War Crimes in Sarajevo, which Dr. Calic also relied upon in a part of her expert opinion. Annex C contains documents which the professor received in the Institute while working on this issue and under item 2 is the population composition of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, a list that this professor made himself on the basis of data obtained. As for annex D, it includes a number of official gazettes of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which were already submitted to this Trial Chamber in Dr. Calic's list, and were used by the professor as well, and this also contains a part of the documentation that the Defence gave to this expert and which he, as he just said in answer to my last question, checked partially and partially felt that it was a sufficient basis for him to make conclusions. As I said at the end, there are four or five documents given to the professor by the Defence and it sought replies in 1992 from these institutions. The professor verified these, but if these four or five documents are an obstacle to the admission of this folder, the Defence proposes immediately that all the documents requested by the Defence from some other institution should be excluded from this folder after which all the documents could be admitted as a basis for the expert's report and opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my client has asked for a five-minute break, if he may beg the court's indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In any event, we should be stopping at 1 o'clock. If it is too much for him to wait, very well. Is it that pressing? If it is not, we will stop at 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I have been so informed by my client. Thank you very much for your understanding, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will rise and let him -- how long would it take him to be ready? We will come back at --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Five minutes, your Honours. If necessary, he can leave and we can continue the discussion. He is just asking permission to leave for five minutes. The Trial Chamber need not rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know what it might turn out to be. We will rise for 10 minutes. 17 18 -- recess taken at 12.40 p.m. to 12.50 p.m. whereupon luncheon adjournment taken -- on resuming at 2.30 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I address the court? Nancy Boler, co-counsel along with Cynthia McMurrey. Ms. McMurrey has felt bad all morning and has got sicker during lunch. With your permission, she has gone back to the hotel to try and get better. Secondly, also during lunch, Mr. Blizzard came in and told me that Mr. Landzo is having some dental problems and that they had arranged for him to see a dentist the day after tomorrow at noon and that he was going to make a request through the Registry that we adjourn court at 11.30 Thursday morning and resume at 2 p.m., to accommodate the dentist. I am sure you will get it in a more formal manner. That is what I was told a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, I acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before breaking for lunch, I had offered these exhibits into evidence. I have no new arguments for the Trial Chamber concerning these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think perhaps at the end of the cross-examination you may renew your application and we will consider it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have completed my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If I can have your indulgence to get situated for a second. You have always been very good about that. May it please the court, good afternoon, professor. We have met. I do not think I have formally introduced myself. My name is Tom Moran. I represent a man named Hazim Delic. He is the last man sitting over there. You do not know Hazim, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sometimes I talk a little fast and sometimes my questions are not as clear as they could be, and so, if you do not understand something I say, will you stop me and we will work with it, and one other thing, if you look there is a lady in black over there and there is a lady in orange over there. They are what are called court reporters. They have to write down everything we say to make a record of the trial, and they cannot write down a nod, so you have to answer "Yes" or "No". You have to answer out loud so historians in the future can look at our record and be able to know what we did here. Okay, professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.
