utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In general I want to discuss with you some things in general and I will go through some of these documents that were presented to you, but just in general I want to talk to you about what historians do and how they work. Sometimes, for instance, you might have what we would call in America an oral history -- you might actually be able to talk to some person who was part of an event. You might be able to talk to George Bush, or Margaret Thatcher and other times you might have to rely on documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So, for instance, if you were doing something on the history of ancient Rome obviously you would have to rely on nothing but documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, when an historian is trained, he is trained to look at documents and determine which documents are reliable, which are relevant, and basically separate the wheat from the chaff; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, as an historian, you would rely on documents prepared by others in reaching your opinions; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That is good, thank you for stopping me. If you were preparing a class, a lecture, writing a book or giving an opinion about something, it would be very common for you to rely on documents that were prepared by other people in reaching those opinions; is that not fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You obviously use documents which have been used by other people, including the historians, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. You might go to the -- if you were doing a history of London, you might go to the British Museum or the British libraries and look at original documents, archives, from years ago, and rely on those kinds of documents to reach your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If the usher could give the witness the volume of maps and the volume of documents and the volume with the report, we might be able to get through this a little bit quicker. (Handed) Professor, let us just start with the volume of maps, because it was on the top of my pile. Let us go to the first map, map M1. You did not prepare that -- I understand -- I know exactly what you are doing, I have been there, looking for the glasses. Map M1, you did not prepare that map, did you, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is a map that was taken over -- it was borrowed from the military encyclopaedia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: This map is the kind of thing that a person of your profession would rely upon in reaching an opinion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head) Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Even though you did not prepare it yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us go to map 2, you did not prepare this map, either, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map was taken from an atlas compiled by a professor in Zagreb, Mr. Ljubo Boban, a member of the academy and I used several of the maps from this atlas, because I considered them reliable and I considered them very well made indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is the kind of thing that a person in your profession would rely on in reaching an opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because there is no need for me to create new maps when there is something already available, which has been an excellent quality work and it contributes to our science and I also knew personally this man, who has since died, but he was an excellent scholar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, we would call that reinventing the wheel -- you do not have to reinvent the wheel every time you want to use one; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us go to map 4, professor. You did not prepare map 4, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know who prepared it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I borrowed this map from another book, which is a published work and I think it reflects the situation as it actually is. It is not as detailed of a map, but it is still detailed enough with respect to what we wanted to show here, which was this project of Serbian lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that is the kind of thing that a person in your profession would rely upon in reaching an opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And map 5, again, you did not prepare this, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is a map from the same atlas which I have mentioned before, compiled by Mr. Ljubo Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it is still the kind of thing that a person in your profession would rely upon in reaching an opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us go to map 6, M6. Again, this is something that someone else prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This map has been published in a book by Suad Arnautovic entitled, "How Bosnia Was Defended".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: This, again, is the kind of thing that a person in your profession would rely upon in reaching an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, if you looked at it carefully, the source of each of these have been indicated on the maps themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I am doing is replying essentially to the objection made by Mr. Niemann and I want to show that each and every one of these documents was one relied upon by this man and secondly is the kind of thing that is relied upon by people in his profession in reaching an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The maps themselves have the sources indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have never disputed at any stage these documents are documents that were relied upon. Right from the very outset I said that. If that is what Mr. Moran is doing, I do not know why, because I have already said it and said it from the start. It has never been disputed that the professor relied on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There is no problem about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think to meet his objections to the admissibility of the documents I think I have to go through each and every one of them and prove not only did he rely upon them but they are the kinds of things a person in his profession would rely upon and they in fact were relied upon in his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think none of this is disputed by even the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If that covers both the maps and the documents in this book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I would not say the same thing as to the documents, but for the maps, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: At this point I would move admission of the book of maps, whatever the exhibit number is. Let us go to the big book and annex A. The first document in annex A is A1, which is a portion of the Bosnian constitution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct -- that is exactly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And is that the current constitution, or is that an earlier constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a version of the constitution under the Austro-Hungarian rule -- this is the Austrian constitution and I think this is actually the original first edition of this constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Professor, obviously you did not prepare that -- it is a constitution of 1880, and obviously someone else prepared that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a constitution which was printed as an official version of the Bosnian constitution in 1910. This is not a later edition and, even if it were a later printing, it would be beyond any doubt -- it is something that originates from that era, so this is an historical document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is clearly the kind of thing that an historian would rely upon in reaching opinions, is it not, professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And in fact you relied upon it in reaching the opinions that you gave in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us move to document A2, which purports to be the constitution of the kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenians -- it has a version in what appears to be Serbian and behind it is an English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is also a stamp there -- the stamp of the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that means that a copy was used that is deposited in the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an historical document and I would like to point you to the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have noticed that, professor. The Bates stamp number on that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that means it has been registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That would be the page that has the stamp at the bottom that says 00013?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is the kind of document that an historian would rely on in reaching opinions -- yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you in fact relied upon that in reaching the opinions that are recorded in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, the next document appears to be a breakdown by population -- that would be document A3 -- which appears to be a breakdown by population group of various religions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, what number are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: A3, and the page would be 20 -- the stamp down at the bottom, 20. Professor I will hold it up and show it to you -- will that help you find it -- this one (indicates).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These tables were prepared on the basis of the official census between 1850 and 1991. All official census data were shown here in which the official State sources were used. There were no private data used -- you can see that 13 different census-taking data were used and I have also given all the pertinent sources for each one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you prepared that chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I prepared this table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it is prepared based on the kinds of documents that people in your profession would rely upon in reaching opinions or giving data; is that a fair assessment, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, you relied on that chart in reaching the opinions that are included in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us go to document A4, which I understand is a resolution of the city of Mostar Muslims in 1941?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Obviously you did not prepare that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But it appears to have come from a printed source of some kind. Is that printed document, the book that this came from the kind of thing that historians would rely on in reaching opinions and in writing books and articles and giving classes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the latest edition of a series of resolutions of the Muslim citizens addressed to the authorities in 1941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought the source was indicated at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I wanted to make sure it is the kind of thing that an historian would rely upon in reaching opinions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not know whether it helps to repeat my position. I thought I made it clear on numerous occasions that the Prosecution has not at any stage suggested that any of this material is not material upon which the professor relied in order to express his opinion. Our objection goes to the truth of the contents of some of the documents -- that is the only issue. So if the exercise that Mr. Moran is now embarking upon is to establish that this material is material that the professor relied upon in order to express his opinion, he is wasting everybody's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am also going to the fact that it is the kind of document that historians and people in his profession rely upon in reaching their opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well and good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If the Prosecutor wants to stipulate that in fact each one of these documents in this book is a document that was relied upon by this witness in reaching his opinion, in fact has included in his opinion and is the kind of document that people in his profession rely upon in reaching opinions, then I think I can stop -- as long as Mr. Niemann is willing to stipulate to all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He is not objecting that these were matters on which an opinion could be based. It is when you rely on it for the truth of what you are saying, then that is where perhaps the problems might arise. He is not disputing that you can rely on it for forming an opinion. The Prosecution is not disputing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He cannot choose for you what you decide to use for your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is true. I want also to show the Trial Chamber, unless Mr. Niemann wants to stipulate to it, that these are the kind of documents that professional historians rely upon in reaching opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is a different matter. We are speaking about this particular historian, and how he reached his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am doing I think two things. One is, did he rely upon it and secondly, is it the kind of documents that professionals in his field -- historians -- rely upon in reaching opinions. If Mr. Niemann is willing to stipulate that it is that, that he relied on them, that they are included in his opinions, then I can stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is up to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He apparently does not want to, so let me continue, your Honour. As to document A4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am prepared to stipulate as long as it is not tendered in evidence as the truth of the contents. I will go further and say that documents -- annexes A through to C, we do not have any particular problems with at all. So, it is the documents that appear in annexe D that we have quite a bit to say about, but up until that point, we have no problems with them either as something that this man relied upon -- which we have never disputed -- or secondly, it is the sort of thing that historians would ordinarily rely on in order to express an opinion. I am not in a position to stipulate to D because I have several arguments about the documents that appear in that category.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think we have taken care of A, B and C. Let us go to D. Professor, if you would flip to annex D way at the back of the book, I believe there are 39 documents in annex D and we will go through them. The first one, which appears to be on document D1 which starts on page 228 -- it appears to be both a Bosnian version and an English translation of a thing called the Izetbegovic/Gligorov platform -- are you familiar with that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Is that the kind of document that historians and people in your profession would rely upon in reaching opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were published in full in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, you did rely upon that document in reaching the opinion that is included in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us go to document D2. That purports to be the declaration of the European Community, recognising Bosnia-Herzegovina, an excerpt from it. Behind it, there seems to be a printed version in English. Is that the kind of document that historians rely upon in reaching opinion -- historians in general -- people in your profession?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is common ground that the European Community recognised it immediately after the referendum of 29 February and 1 March. It is an admitted position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Actually, this is dated 6 April -- this document is dated 6 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Immediately after the referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 6 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Bosnia declared itself a Republic in the first week of February -- I think 5 February and the European Community recognised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The only reason I am doing this is because there seems to be some question about whether these are the kind of documents -- annex D are the kinds of documents that historians rely upon in reaching their opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Some of these documents you will find in Dr. Calic's report, also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct, but Mr. Niemann has not designated which specific documents in annex D he thinks are not the kinds of documents historians rely upon in reaching their opinions, or that this man relied upon in reaching his opinion. Without knowing otherwise, I think I have to go through all 39 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Almost all of them are public documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Published in the gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- published there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I agree with you 100 per cent. I think that they are clearly the kind of documents that historians would rely upon in reaching opinions, and that this witness relied upon in reaching his opinion as an historian. I think that -- I absolutely agree with you, your Honour. But given the Prosecution's position, I am afraid I have to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I cannot understand why Mr. Moran has to do this. The documents are sought to be tendered by Madam Residovic. Is this some sort of a cooperative effort in an extension of evidence-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a second? I want to discuss what we discussed last night in closed session for about two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I can indicate the ones to which we would want present argument as to why they ought not be admissible. They are Exhibit D21, and all of the documents contained in Exhibit D21 -- not Exhibit D21, document D21; D31; D32; D33; D34; D35; D36; D37; D38; and D39. We are not objecting, but we believe that there has been no foundation laid in terms of the source of documents D8, D10 and D12 to 22. They are not necessarily objected to, that last group, but there is no indication of the source of them at all. If that assists the Chamber, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose this can be established in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Then I am presuming, if I understood correctly, and I hope the Trial Chamber corrects me if I misunderstood, it seems to be everybody's position that documents 1 through 7, 9, 11, 23, 24, 25, and then 26 through 30 are the kinds of documents that historians would normally rely on in reaching their opinions and that this man in fact did do that, and that there is not going to be any objection to those coming in. Did I understand that correctly, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose what the Prosecution is saying -- not only that, all of them -- but he is objecting to the source and authority of these other documents which he complains about. Any other document which might have been used could be used for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me go through them quickly and see if we can take care of those. Let us start with document D8. The first page of that has number 293 on the bottom of it. That purports to be the minutes of the 9th session of the Konjic municipal Parliament. Where did you get those documents, professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has -- this document has been authenticated, it has the registration number, the stamp of the municipal assembly -- it is an authentic document that one can rely on, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is the kind of document that appears to be authentic -- it does not appear to be a forgery, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is the kind of document that an historian would rely upon in reaching his opinion -- historians in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are valuable documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you in fact relied upon it in reaching your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us skip to document D10, professor. D10 purports to be the conclusions from the joint meeting of the war presidency in Konjic defence force's command dated 18 May 1992. I notice that that has a seal on it, also -- the original in Bosnian. Do you know where this document came from, professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is a document I received from the institute, and I think it is authentic, and I used it because it is an invaluable document which can easily be checked -- it is signed by the president of the presidency, with the stamp and date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you say "the institute", what do you mean by "the institute" -- which institute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean the Institute for the Investigation of War Crimes -- crimes against humanity and international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And who runs that institute, professor -- who funds it, who pays for it, who is in charge of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an institute financed by the State.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it collects documents related to allegations of war crimes and atrocities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the history of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it is put together so that historians in future years can go there and see what happened in Bosnia from 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And so these documents would be the kind -- document D10 would be the kind of document that an historian -- not only today but maybe 100 years from now, would rely upon in reaching an opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you in fact relied upon it in reaching your opinions that are contained in your report here; is that correct, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I also believe it to be an authentic document and a very valuable one for future studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And let us go to document number D12. That purports to be the order of the war presidency to Radio Konjic dated 21 May 1992. I notice that -- your Honours, it is page 323 in the book. It also has a seal on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And where did you get this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received this document from the Defence council offices, and I think it is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Why do you think it is an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so because I have reviewed several such documents and I have that much experience to be able to tell what is authentic and what is not. This is a document which has all the necessary characteristics of documents of this type that were issued at the time. There is a heading, who is sending it to whom, the registration number, the date, a signature -- it has all the characteristics of an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And so it is the kind of document that an historian would rely upon in reaching opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it is in fact a document you relied upon in reaching your opinions that are contained in the report that has been tendered to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us go to document number D13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That purports to be the decision on establishment of the commission for the issues of killed, injured and missing persons from the Konjic war presidency, dated 25 May 1992. Do you know where that document came from?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just comment? This exhibit has already been admitted into evidence and it is a document that the witness was given by the Defence, but it is already included in the evidence -- admitted by this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As exhibit what -- what is the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Through witness Djajic. I am afraid I cannot remember the number, but we will look it up and let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: While they are looking that one up we will skip that one and go to the next one and save some time. Let us go to document D14. That purports to be the conclusions of the war presidency dated 3 June 1992. Where did you get that document, professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got this document, too, from the Defence counsel. And I consider it, too, to be authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Does it have the indicia of authenticity for documents that you would normally see in the Bosnian Government -- things like seals and registration numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hold it to be an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that is based on your experience and training in dealing with documents from the Bosnian Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And this is the kind of document that historians would rely upon in reaching conclusions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you in fact relied upon it in reaching your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The conclusions that are in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us go to D15. That purports to be the order of the war presidency to provide the necessary number of blankets for the prisoners at the Celebici facility, dated 3 June 1992. Where did you get it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next group of documents was also given to me by the Defence counsel and they follow on to the document we have previously discussed, so that all the decisions were typed separately as instructions to certain institutions, which are required to carry out the tasks assigned to them, so that this is nothing new that is being referred to; it is just a specification of the individual tasks for various municipal bodies, so it is nothing new that they contain. If the previous one is admitted, then there is no point in questioning these.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am afraid I have to. So D15 bears the indicia of being an original -- a copy of an authentic Bosnian Government document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And this is the kind of document that historians rely upon in reaching opinions and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you in fact relied upon it in reaching your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Professor, let us go to D16, which will be on page 339. That is the order of the war presidency to send detainees to medical checks, dated 3 June 1992. Again, does this bear the indicia of reliability, that it shows -- it has got the form that a Bosnian Government document would have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And an historian who was handed this document would find it sufficiently reliable to base his opinions, at least in part, on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you in fact relied upon that document in reaching your opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us go to D17. This purports to be the order of the Konjic war presidency to the Konjic ministry of the interior on the control of vehicles, again dated 3 June 1992. Again, I presume this came from Ms. Residovic's office -- that is how you got it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But looking at this document, it bears the indicia of reliability; that is, it looks like what a Bosnian Government document would look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it has the seals and it has the registration numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it has -- for someone who is used to dealing with these documents, they would accept this as an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And an historian could base his opinions on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you in fact also did -- you based your opinions at least in part on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: D18 purports to be the decision of the Konjic war presidency on the making of a list of civilians in Donje Selo and Bradina and it is dated 3 June. Again, this document came from Ms. Residovic to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And from looking at it and from looking at the registration numbers and the way it is laid out and the signatures and such things, does that appear to you to be an authentic document from the war presidency in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it is the kind of document that a person in your profession would rely upon in reaching opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you in fact relied upon it in reaching your opinions that are contained in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The next one is D19 and that is the decision of the Konjic war presidency on the members, dated 26 October 1992. Where did you get this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received this document, too, from the office of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, from looking at the document, it looks like an authentic Bosnian Government document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it has enough indicia of reliability that an historian would rely upon it in reaching an opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you in fact relied upon it in reaching your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Document D20, that purports to be a BiH army pamphlet on the obligations to respect the rules of war and the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we seem to have skipped a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We have? Which one did we skip?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There seem to be two documents in D19. It starts 349 through to 356.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Professor, can you go to page 348 in the documents? It is a copy of the Bosnian original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Does that appear to be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: An authentic Bosnian document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If I read you part of an English translation and I will just -- just a couple of lines, could you check it against the Bosnian to make sure we are reading off the same thing. I am going to be reading from page 353 in the book. It starts off: "Dear Sirs, having in mind your duties and responsibility during the war ......" I know that Bosnian is very hard to read.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a text, so there might be slight differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I have been informed because we did not provide a text to the interpreters there might be slight differences in translation. The document on 348 and the document on page 353 appear to be the same -- just translation --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, your Honours, but I am not getting the interpretation for a couple of minutes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do the interpreters themselves have these documents? I am not sure they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I was not planning on reading any of them. Apparently what we have is a cover letter followed by a longer letter -- the longer document -- I wanted to make sure everybody agreed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It gives the membership of the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour and then there is a document behind it -- the first is a cover letter, and the second is a decision on who is the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is 349.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In the Bosnian version it starts off at 349 and runs through page 352. The English translation would be on page 354 and runs to page 356, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Those are the same documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I believe we were on D20. Just so the record is clear, on annex D, document 19, both the cover letter and the decision appear to be authentic Government documents from the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And they bear sufficient indicia of reliability that an historian would rely upon those in reaching his decisions and opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you in fact did on yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This document is dated 26 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. Document D20, where did you get that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are several similar documents to -- similar to this in the archives. These are the leaflets being handed out to the soldiers in an exercise or in preparation for a particular operation where the soldiers are warned of the Geneva Conventions and respecting them, because our Government issued several orders in that regard and even trained its personnel in order to prevent any kind of violation of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So these would be handed out to combat troops right before an operation, or people going through some sort of a training programme -- is that where these were used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: This is the kind of document that a person in your profession would rely upon in reaching opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You are starting to get used to the questions -- you are anticipating me and you are doing it correctly. You in fact relied upon this document in reaching your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us go to D21. That is the order of the TO defence municipal headquarters and the Croat Council of Defence restricting entrance into the houses of Serbs, plunder of property and cattle, dated 6 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Where did you get the Bosnian version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received it from the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Looking at the document as a whole, does it appear to be an authentic document or a copy of an authentic document from the Bosnian Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it has sufficient marks and indicia of reliability, the way it is laid out and the signatures and everything that an historian would take --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: -- this document to be an authentic document and rely upon it in arriving at opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Behind that, there appears to be a second document which somehow apparently was not marked, at least in my copy. It is on page 364. There is another document on page 366, 367, 368, 369, 370, 371, 372, 373, 374, 375, 376, 377, 378, 379, 380, 381, 382, 383, 384, 385 -- it looks like it goes back through about page 466.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed, there are 130 of them, your Honour, and some of them are totally illegible. None of them are in the English language or the French language. So, I cannot see how we can have any discussion of them until we know what they have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are authentic documents, which have been given to us by the Institute for Research of the War Crimes and Violations of Humanitarian Law. They have all been authenticated and they have all been registered, all of these documents, to the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: They are the kinds of documents --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are all authentic documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which ones are you discussing now -- authentic documents -- we do not know what kind they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What kind of documents are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object to this. This is highly irregular. We are discussing documents and we have no idea what they are. Counsel knows full well these documents are supposed to be translated into an official language of the Tribunal and made available to the parties. He cannot come here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, you cannot defend that. You can see that there is no way of knowing what these documents represent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. At this point, all I am attempting to prove through this witness -- remember, this is not my exhibit, I got this exhibit Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: All I am trying to prove through this witness is that they are the kinds of documents -- the basic kinds of documents they are, and his familiarity with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you really seriously yourself saying that? You do not even know what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How can you say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I cannot say they are authentic documents, your Honour. I have absolutely no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Why do you put up such a proposition to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We will jump ahead to document D22, your Honour, which purports to be the report of the BiH army military police on the transfer of detainees from the Celebici prison into the sports gymnasium prison. The Bosnian version would be on page 450 and the English translation is on 451 and 452.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me look for 450 and 451. Very well -- 450 and 452.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: 452 would be the English translation of the Bosnian document in 450.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is a continuation -- 450, 452 are the same document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact the index on this is wrong, is it not -- this is not the report of the BiH army police, but in fact it is a constitutional amendment to the Bosnian constitution; is that not right? It is a decision from the presidency of the Republic of BiH --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of the presidency, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it appears to be out of, what, the official gazette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is a decision on the establishment of a State commission on collecting facts on war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that is the kind of document --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are not objecting. Our concern was that we could not understand what the index meant in relation to this document. Now that has been clarified, we have no further problems with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us jump ahead to document D31, which would be on page 509. That purports to be a certification from the Konjic municipality related to a man named Zejnil Delalic. Does that appear to you to be an official document, or a copy of an official document from the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Is it the kind of document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: -- that an historian would rely upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You in fact relied upon it in arriving at your opinions that are contained in your report. Your Honour, it is on page -- the English is on page 511, your Honours. In fact, what this document says is that there is no record of certain events occurring; is that not what document D31 says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you relied upon it in reaching your decisions and your opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it is the kind of thing historians in general would use to write books or articles, to reach opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an official source. Therefore, it is based on particular books and certain registries, which are of the official type.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And historians rely on those kind of records in reaching opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it does not make any difference whether you are an historian from the United States, from Bosnia, from England or Germany or Russia -- wherever -- these are the kinds of documents that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: -- a trained historian might use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us go to D32, which purports to be a document from the district military court in Mostar dated 16 May 1996. It appears to be a certification from the President of the court -- the chairman of the court, excuse me -- related to a man named Zejnil Delalic. Does the Bosnian original bear the indicia of reliability?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: This would be the kind of document -- the kind of public official record that historians would rely upon in reaching their opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you in fact relied upon it to reach your opinion that is given in this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am just wondering whether Mr. Moran intends to seek to admit this in his own case. That is what he said the basis of these questions are -- this and the other documents that relate to Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not sure what I intend to admit but I sure want to prove them all up before I let this witness go. I cannot prove up the authenticity of these documents and their admissibility, and given that, once this witness has gone, we cannot -- I guess we could get him back but it would be a waste of time if I missed one of these exhibits that I wanted to admit, that there seemed to be some dispute over, and then we would have to send him another plane ticket from Sarajevo and bring him back here and slow the whole process down. At this point all I am doing is proving the admissibility of evidence -- I am not moving it, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would observe, your Honour, that it does not prove the truth of the contents of the document. It merely proves that he relied on it and, as your Honour observed on numerous occasions, if this sort of evidence is to be admitted, then the people who are best competent to admit it should be called to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us go to D33. That seems to be another document related to a man named Zejnil Delalic from Jablanica. Does that appear to be an official document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And is it the kind of document that is sufficiently reliable that an historian would rely upon it in reaching an opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, did you rely upon it in reaching an opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Document number 34 purports to be from the Jablanica SDA saying that they do not have a record that someone is a member -- a named individual is a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received this from the Defence counsel's office and I believe that it has all the features of an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I notice just from looking at it that even the SDA Party seals documents and it seems to me that at least in the former Yugoslavia everybody had a seal and they were used much more than they are in my country to authenticate documents; is that correct -- every different office has its own seal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that is one of the indicia of reliability, that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And did you rely upon this letter in reaching your opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it is the kind of thing that an historian would rely upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because there is no counter document, or an opposing document, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Document number D35 is another letter from the -- it appears to be the Muslim Bosnian cultural circle to Ms. Residovic. This appears to be what it purports to be, does it not -- a letter from the Vienna Community of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You have to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it is the kind of document that is reliable enough that if an historian would rely upon it in reaching an opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The next one is D36, which purports to be an excerpt from the SDA Vienna cultural circle statute. In fact, all that anyone is tendering is an excerpt from that, which is on -- the English version is on page 535 -- that is all anyone is interested in. Does this document, D36, appear to be a document that is sufficiently reliable that an historian would rely upon it in reaching his opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have all the elements for authentication here. I did not study this document. It only has a title but nobody signed it, nobody registered it -- it is not clear as to when it was recorded and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you rely upon it in reaching any opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Is that because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was interesting for the expert study, but I did not go into this period very much, so, if needs be, this document can also be eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Jumping ahead to the next group of documents, which are D37. They appear to be certificates from the secretariat for general administration in Konjic related to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: -- people's citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If you do not know the answer to this, "I do not know" is a fine answer. In different countries, the evidence that you were born some place or your citizenship is somewhere may come from different Government agencies. I will give you an example. My birth certificate which proves where I was born is kept by the Health Department, but my passport would come from the State Department, our foreign ministry. On the other hand, if someone were a naturalised citizen in my country the records would come from the Justice Department, so there are all various different places. Is this Government organisation the secretariat for general administrative inspection the kind of Government agency that would keep records relating to a person's citizenship and nationality. By "nationality" I do not mean ethnic group; by "nationality" I mean a tie to a State or Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the question on the grounds that the document relates to citizenship, not nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Fine. Is this organisation, the secretariat for general administrative inspection, the kind of Government agency in Bosnia-Herzegovina that would keep official Government records of whether or not a person was a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The certificates of citizenship are issued by the municipal Governments and one of the agencies there is the general administration department and, to me, it is an authentic document, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So, if you went to wherever your citizenship is registered, and wanted a document to prove that you were a citizen of BiH, that you would get a document that looks something like this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And there are several of them in here. I would ask you to flip through them. They refer to various people. I will not read their names for several reasons, not the least of which I think at least one of them is a protected witness. If you would look through those documents in those copies, would you tell me if those are -- if they appear to be what they purport to be, that is, documents of citizenship -- showing citizenship in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I verified these documents in the Konjic municipality -- I did verify these documents, and I consider them to be authentic documents. I verified them there, in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you went to the municipal building yourself and looked at the original records?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, in your opinion, these things are the real McCoy -- the real thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And are these the kinds of documents that historians in general would rely upon in arriving at opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And did you rely upon these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we are between documents, I think it is 3 minutes to 4. This may be a convenient time to break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you got to the last document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I will hang in there and get them all done before the break. D38, this purports to be a report of the general hospital in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Involving casualties. Where did you get this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document that the Defence received from the general hospital in Konjic on the number of people who were injured, wounded or killed during the war, who were treated in the hospital -- whether they were brought to the hospital or whatever -- in whichever way they had been brought there, and who were treated there, whether they were civilian or military, including the killed ones, so this is not the total of all casualties in the area -- only those who were processed through the hospital, who in some way were registered there. For instance, a total number of injured civilians and the total number of injured military personnel, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And this looks like the kind of document that a hospital would generate -- would make -- it has the seal, it has again those indicia of reliability?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He says it was issued to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I thought he said it was -- he got it from the Defence lawyer. I may have misheard. It was issued to you by the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How did you get it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received it from the Defence counsel's office, but I believe it is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact there are some things that you can look at inside the document to aid you in determining whether or not it is authentic, not just the seal but the numbers for instance, the total number of people who were treated, given the other knowledge you have about the Konjic area during the war, would those be reasonable numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it would be the kinds of numbers you would expect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, if the numbers were well away from anything you expected, then you would not consider the document reliable; is that right? Maybe I phrased that question badly. Let me try again, okay, professor? If the numbers of wounded reported were much higher or much lower than you would expect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know the need for that. Whether he disputes it or not he based his opinion on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I was also trying to get to the reliability of the document. We can skip on to the next one. The last one is document number 39, which appears to be something from the Konjic municipal secretariat for displaced persons. Does that appear to be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: -- an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: From the Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you rely upon this in reaching your decision, your opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And an historian, just in general, who was presented with this document, would he rely upon it in reaching his opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few more questions, but I think I have got to the end of this book. This may be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will rise now and return at 4.30. -- recess taken at 4.03 p.m. 7 -- on resuming at 4.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, your Honour, there seemed to be some question about at least two of the documents -- I think the Prosecution questioned their authenticity. The two I am thinking about right off the bat are D13 and D19, the ones that are in this as documents D13 and D19. D13 as I understand it is a document which was seized at INDA-BAU and was D71/1. Document D19, where the Prosecutor also questioned the authenticity, has previously been introduced into evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 72.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As to Prosecution Exhibit 72, I will not vouch for its authenticity. I will let Mr. Niemann do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was a minor confusion. I asked my colleague, Tom, to comment on D13. It has already been admitted into evidence as D71/1 through Fadil Zebic. It is not a document coming from INDA-BAU, whereas D19 has been admitted as Prosecution Exhibit 72 through the witness Dr. Calic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I stand corrected, your Honour, as to D13. I must have must understood and I apologise to the court for any misunderstanding I may have had. I thank Ms. Residovic for correcting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think the witness is now in the stand, so you can continue with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Professor, a couple of other things and I will direct your attention to a series of documents, starting at D31, and running through I believe D35. I may have some more beyond that. These, on their face, purport to be documents provided by officials of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Ms. Residovic at her request. Page 510 is the first one, professor. We will just start at that one and use that one for an example and I will go through the others very, very quickly. Professor, I am going to give you an example from my country and see if you know the answer to this and, if you do, fine and if you do not, that is fine, too. It is possible, in my country, to go to a Government agency and say, "Has Tom Moran ever been convicted of a crime?" So, for instance, I could go, or you could go to the court clerk's office in my home county and, for the grand total I think of $5 get a letter addressed to you, saying that the district clerk had searched the records and found that I have never been convicted -- no record that I have ever been convicted of a crime. They would seal it. That would be an official record of the court. Can you do that kind of thing in Bosnia, go to a court clerk, or a Government official and say, "We have searched our records and we do not find a record of this."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one can obtain such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And basically what it is, it is a certificate from the Government custodian of records that certain records do not exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And so, for instance, on D31, which we just looked at, it says that there is no records of Mr. Delalic occupying any position in the Government of Konjic in 1992. That does not mean that he did not -- that just means there is no record of it; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the next one, D32, appears to be a certificate from the district military court in Mostar that there are no criminal records in that court involving a man named Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the next one, which would be D33, is from the Mostar security police, Konjic police station, saying that they have no criminal records involving a man named Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And those would be the kinds of things that anybody could go in and pay, whatever the fee is -- whatever the set fee is and get it on anybody. Let me phrase that a little clearer. You could go into the clerk's office in the court in my home town and, for $5, get a letter from the clerk --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object. I do not think the witness has shown any evidence at all that he knows anything about the United States or the practice there in relation to the issue of certificates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose this is merely using it as a comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the purpose of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has had some objection to these documents based on the fact that they are addressed to Ms. Residovic and I am just trying to show through this witness that these are the kinds of documents that anybody can get from the appropriate Government official saying that records do not exist. It is irrelevant whether they are addressed to Ms. Residovic or Mr. Niemann or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose what the Prosecutor is saying, you might have got such documents from her and he might have based his opinion on them, but the fact whether the contents are true is a different matter, which he is not prepared to argue. That is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What I am trying to prove up is that these kinds of documents showing the lack of a public record, or a business record -- the next one I have is a record of a business -- that those kinds of records or documents are commonly available and that these appear to be documents that show the custodian of records searched for records and could not find them. We will use this one as an example. The next one is D34, of which the Bosnian version is on page 519. It appears to be a certificate under seal from the SDA Party that a man named Zejnil Delalic is not a former member of the Party, has not been elected to the Party -- there are no records of that. Things other than governments, like businesses in Bosnia-Herzegovina, do they commonly give certificates that, "We have searched our business records and we find no record of so and so," whoever it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that, because I am not a member of the Party and I never asked for such certificates, so I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Professor, I do not know -- unlike one of your exams in your classes, "I do not know" can be a very proper answer in a courtroom, if you do not know. At this point I will pass the witness and I thank the court very much for its indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other cross-examination by Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, may it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good afternoon, professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: My name is Zeljko Olujic. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. We will not take long. You must be tired by now, but let us just clear up a few points that emerge from your testimony before this honourable court. You spoke about the escalation of the crisis in SFRY, so I should like us to clear up something that cannot be seen from your written report or from your oral testimony in court. Who had the majority in Kosovo in 1988, could you clear that up a little?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Albanians are in a majority in Kosovo -- 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that Milosevic's gain of control over Kosovo, Montenegro and Vojvodina resulted in fundamental legal and political changes, but that it had repercussions throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia, could we say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, professor, who was the BiH representative in the presidency of Yugoslavia by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Regarding the culmination of the crisis, as you described it in your statement, could you explain the emergence of the Serbian Radical Party led by Vojslov Seselj with a little more detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The role of the Radical Party of Vojslov Seselj, which was based in Ruma and in Belgrade, was one of the elements of the policy of Slobodan Milosevic. He sought, through such radical elements, to interfere in the crisis in Bosnia, to radicalise elements in Bosnia, to send paramilitary formations there. Arkan and his men played a similar role .

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, professor, regarding the Serbian paramilitary organisations, they existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but can we say that they existed in Kosovo, Serbia, Montenegro, and in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. If I am not mistaken I said in my testimony that they existed in the Knin, Krajina, in Eastern Slovonia, in Western Srem and in Baranje, this encouragement of radical tendencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: One further point, professor, regarding the chapter dealing with the influence of neighbouring States on the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, could you tell us who was the first in the world to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The European Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: After that, among the States?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The United States of America and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you, professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. Olujic. Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: No questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, have you any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, in your report at page 14, and I have the English version of it only, so I am not sure that the -- if your version is in English or in Bosniak, but perhaps you might take the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have either version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might be given your version of the report. (Handed) Is your version in the English language, professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have it also in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you read English, professor, or do you only read Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On page 14, the first paragraph -- the first full paragraph -- starts, "as an answer the Serb representatives in the Parliament".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may start by reminding him of the heading -- I think that is a continuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is under (b), "Development of the Situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the Election in 1990" -- thank you, your Honour. Then, on page 14, in the English version, "As an answer the Serb representatives in the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina" -- do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The second paragraph on 14.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, page 14 of my document does not seem to be what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is why we preferred using the title heading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The difference, the culmination of the crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Go to, "The Political Processes in Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1990 to 1992."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (b), "Development of the Situation in BiH after elections 1990". It is from there that you can trace it to the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can take over from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the first free elections?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, this is the tenth paragraph in my English version. I have not been given a Serbo-Croat version -- not that I could read it anyway, but I cannot assist by going to that. Perhaps I can come at it another way, rather than showing you a report. In my version it says: "As an answer the Serb representatives in the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina founded the assembly of Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina on 24 November." The date 24 November, can you help me with where you got that date from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says 24 October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: November here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think it is a mis-translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "November" has been mis-translated, thank you. Going into the next section, do you see the heading, (c), "International Recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina" and then there is seven paragraphs and then you mention the Ram Plan. You say: "In media there were pieces of information about the Ram Plan by which the State and military leaders." Et cetera. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, have you ever seen the Ram Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know of anyone who has actually studied it or produced any material on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This Ram Plan figured in the press and its borders, its frameworks were mentioned, but I personally have not seen the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know of anyone who has?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I know quite a number of people from -- even some people from the general staff -- the former general staff, but I did not have occasion to discuss this with them, because these are people who have left the army a long time ago, so I could not really testify to the effect that I know exactly what the Ram Plan envisaged, though it was referred to in the press and even in some books, according to which this Ram Plan was a programme of Greater Serbia, which was to be achieved and the border, which went as far as Karlobag, Virovitica, Karlovac, that that actually was that plan, covering the Serbian people in Yugoslav territories and in fact this is an old programme designed for the creation of Greater Serbia and it is almost 200 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is something that you acquired from looking at the media reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is what he says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But it reflects the historical territory that the Serbs claimed for their land, for their State.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mention further on, four paragraphs down from there, you make mention to the proclamation of the referendum results by President Izetbegovic and then you say on the 4 April the European Community recognised Bosnia, et cetera. Are you saying there that, in your opinion, that is when Bosnia became an independent sovereign State, or are you not saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
