utterances.text: Bosnia -- not when the referendum was held but when it was internationally recognised and it was internationally recognised on 6 March. President Izetbegovic asked the international community to recognise the sovereignty and independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A month after that, that is, on 6 April, the European Community actually recognised it -- the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is the independence day which Bosnia-Herzegovina is celebrating to this day, and the following day it was recognised by the United States of America and the Republic of Croatia and then other States followed. Today, there are more than 200 that have recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Moving on to the next paragraph, paragraph (d), "Beginning of War Operations against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and the second to last paragraph in that section there, you speak of the transformation of the JNA in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in mid May; do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This change brought about nothing --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Middle of May, middle of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The middle of May the JNA was transformed into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On 27 April, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was proclaimed and it recognised the army, which was in Bosnia, to be its proper army. However, since then, the soldiers who were born in Bosnia but served in the JNA, were transferred to the army of the Republika Srpska, so, according to the testimony of General Kadijevic, between 60,000 and 80,000, and according to the commander of the second military district, General Kukanjac --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I could stop you for a moment, because my question is a very short one. I do not want you to recite the whole history of that. I really want you to tell me, in your opinion, what was the impetus that brought about that transformation -- why did it take place -- that is all I want to know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This came about because, at that time, this army had to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina. The United Nations called for its withdrawal and then only the soldiers who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Further in your report, and under the heading (f), "Measures and Activities of the Legal Power, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is the ninth paragraph of that report, you talk about the problems of printing and distributing the official gazettes in which the laws and provisions were published; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head) Yes, I do see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also make reference to the constitutional court intervening with a decision that the laws would be applied from the moment they were delivered. I just ask you, professor, some of these laws were printed and distributed very late, were they not, in 1992 -- in some cases, they were several months in getting out because of the siege of Sarajevo that was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But I included in the material a report, which concerns this problem, where the constitutional court asked for an explanation, that is, the official gazette was asked why these laws are being delayed, why their publishing was being delayed and the difficulties were of a different nature. On the one hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In those cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- it was impossible to print, so the printing itself was a problem. There was a problem of procuring paper, a problem of electric power, different kinds of shortages and problems that could not be solved, so that the official gazette was late -- either 30 days because of certain reasons, three months because of different other reasons, and these copies were arriving very late and different methods were used for them to be brought out of Sarajevo. At one point, they were printed in Zenica and so on, so different methods were used in order to get the official gazette through to the institutions which were supposed to get them. So, there were major problems there and there were delays, even of several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In those cases, the municipality would have either had to operate under old law, or to improvise and function as best it could -- would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed, I think you go on in the next paragraph to say that the problem was even further exacerbated by the communication difficulties from particularly Sarajevo to the municipal regions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed, it would be true to say, would it not, professor, that, in some areas, in the early stages, the municipal authority was the only available authority to deal effectively with the whole range of matters that confronted the municipality, including military matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the military communications are something else and I think that they should be distinguished from the distribution of the official gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, why then, on page -- my page 23, under the heading (5), "Organisation of Civil Authorities in the Konjic Municipality", (a), "Peacetime Authorities", you see a reference there: "Along with passing regulations, municipal assembly had a very important role in regard to appointing municipal leading officials." Et cetera. Then you say: "The officers in the municipal bodies, magistrates and commander of the OSTO." Or the municipal Territorial Defence headquarters -- that is a military matter, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not follow you, I could not find the text. I do not know what it is about. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means. You were saying --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is the title, by the way?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is called heading (5), "Organisation of Civil Authorities in the Konjic Municipality" and then, "Peacetime Authorities Organisations"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that you say there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- that the commander of the municipal Territorial Defence is appointed by the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He is proposed by them, but further on it states that he is confirmed by the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you saying that my translation is wrong, that it does not say that, "along with the passing of regulations, the municipal assembly," et cetera, "had a role in regard to appointing" and then it mentions a number of bodies and then it says, "the commander of the municipal Territorial Defence and the commander of the municipal headquarters of civil protection and others" -- is my translation wrong there, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object. This relates to the peacetime circumstances and this is what I see both in the original and in the translation. There is another heading, another chapter, which discusses these issues in wartime circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you not think that the expert can handle that himself? It is a simple thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was only in March and April. What I provided in my chart for the organisational structure of the authority was only for March and April, that the municipal assembly is in charge of appointing the military personnel, whereas, later on, it is moved to the republican authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "later on", perhaps you might help us with the time. Are you saying that the municipal authorities, if I may call them that, did not appoint the commander of the TOs, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was that, when did they cease to appoint the commanders of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stopped appointing the commander of the Territorial Defence when the old Territorial Defence ceased to exist and the new Territorial Defence was established. That is the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence -- and the general staff of the Territorial Defence was established and this was later transformed into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so this was valid for a very short period of time. It was valid only in the beginning. However, later on, it becomes part of the republican staff for the Territorial Defence authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I might come back to that in a moment. Going on to page 25, under paragraph (6), "Plans and Activities of the SDS" et cetera, the first paragraph there, you say that: "The local Serbs counted on a very important support of the Yugoslav People's Army and they assumed that central SDS bodies in Bosnia-Herzegovina would help them." It is true, is it not, that many of the Serb people regarded the JNA as their legitimate army -- as the legitimate army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, but there is a discrepancy between -- okay, the activities of the Serbian Democratic Party is the activity of the SDS at the beginning of the war -- is that the heading that you are looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, do you want me to repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What I am saying to you is that many of the local Serbs went further than just relying on the support of the Yugoslav People's Army -- many of them in fact regarded it as their legal, legitimate army, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- while they were arming it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, in a similar vein, they considered the territory that they occupied as part of either a federation of the old Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or as part of Greater Serbia, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were still within Bosnia-Herzegovina -- they were still not talking about a Greater Serbia -- they were still in Yugoslavia, so they were playing a double game. They were for a long time within the institutions of the whole system, but secretly they were working on organising their own power and to protect their own interests, so a question phrased in this way is partial and it would require a lengthier explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is an important matter, professor, so if you think that you need to give a lengthier answer, please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you expanded your question properly -- whether their wish is merely an intention or they were actually demonstrating sufficient activity to justify the fact that they preferred a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. My question was directed perhaps to a slightly different issue, your Honour, but I will ask the question perhaps again, but in a slightly different way. My question, professor, is that many of the local Serbs considered themselves either to be part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or, failing that, that their territory was part of Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I say here is that the Serbs do not talk openly of a Greater Serbia -- they are talking about the organisation of power within Bosnia-Herzegovina and they want to join Serbia. That is their goal. What kind of a State that will be, whether that would be Yugoslavia, Greater Serbia, in the final analysis it would be a Greater Serbia, just as the others wanted, as these autonomous districts in Croatia wanted. It was a similar case to that in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- a whole system of power is being built there and they are trying to build a position in Bosnia, because they were aware that they could not change the decision on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was adopted in April and that the borders can only be changed by means of war, so this war started and it was not -- and what they wanted to achieve was not possible without a war, so that is the crux of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am aware of that, professor. I do not want to cut you off, but the point that I am getting to was that not what you would say was the legal reality in terms of borders. I am asking you questions about what the intention of the Serbian -- local Serbian people was, particularly in the Konjic municipality -- sorry, I withdraw that -- the local Serbian people in Bosnia was -- not all of them, but some of them. Perhaps I can assist you. What other meaning can be given to that than what you say in the last paragraph of the section (a), "Activities of the SDS Before the Attack Against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina" -- and that is on page 27, if your Honours please -- where you say: "The SDS intention to divide the Konjic municipality and to include the area called the Serb Konjic municipality into the Greater Serbia project was acknowledged in the form of an official document by the above mentioned decision." What else could you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, but again I am unable to find this. I believe that our different copies are completely differently numbered, so could you please maybe point me to the heading again and then ask your question again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Paragraph 6, the last paragraph in 6 before you get to (b) -- the last paragraph. (6) is, "Plans and Activities of the SDS Before and at the Beginning of the War in 1992". Then, before you get to (b), the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "By this decision and the SDS is trying to divide the territory of the municipality of Konjic and annex it to the Serb republic" -- is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please restate your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that not an expression of an intention by the local Serbian people to be part of Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is a fact, is it not, professor, that the JNA armed many of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that happened not only -- and that happened in places such as Konjic as well as other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, in fact, there was very direct contact and relationship between the local Serbian people -- some of the local Serbian people -- and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, I wish to move on to the next section, which is paragraph (7), "The Plans and Activities of the HDZ" et cetera and I will ask you some questions about that, if I may. What was the State or Republic of origin of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but there was also the HDZ as a national ruling Party in Croatia that won the elections there -- it has the same name. But, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HDZ started not as a branch but as the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is a Party of the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the HVO is the military arm of the HDZ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO was not the military arm of the HDZ; it is the military and civilian factor of authority of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which, again, was organised under the leadership of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it legal under the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time for political parties or communities to have their own armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The legal authorities and the Parliament of Bosnia proclaimed both paramilitary formations that were illegal and unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, the Republika Srpska on which the Parliament passed a decision and the constitutional court proclaimed that the decisions taken by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna on 19 November 1991 and on 3 July 1992 were unconstitutional and nine such documents were specified and they were proclaimed to be unlawful, unconstitutional, but the Bosnian authorities did not take any steps to remedy the situation that had occurred with the foundation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Why? Because the legal authorities were under very heavy pressure of the combat against the Serbs and they did not wish to open up a second front. That is one reason. A second is that Croatia was among the first to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina; it accepted refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina; and we had to rely on Croatia if we wanted to receive humanitarian aid, food, or armament -- we had to rely on Croatia. The legal authorities did not wish to engage in a conflict with the HVO, or Herceg-Bosna, or with the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But the expediency and perhaps justifiable expediency of not taking action against military or paramilitary organisations such as the HVO did not affect the question of its illegality -- am I right in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna continued to exist via facti -- in fact -- but things will change when the first conflicts start and those were those that affected Konjic, the attack on Prozor, and that was when the situation became very strained between the HVO and the legal authorities in Konjic, and this would later, in 1993, lead to a conflict between the HVO and the BiH Army, which, again, would be an extremely difficult problem for the legal authorities and for the Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We might adjourn and start at 10 o'clock tomorrow morning. 9 10

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 12 5.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, 13 the 1st day of April 1998, at 10 a.m.
